rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about proof and risk; it turns thin facts into testable questions instead of dressing them up for the ballroom. Its strongest line is, "This reporter will want the number, the definition, and whether it survives a selection-effect challenge" -- that is exactly the nasty follow-up a real retail reporter asks. A has the punchier hook in "Warby Parker bets its future on the stores it was built to disrupt," but then it overreaches with claims like "retail beats online-only" and "sells glasses better than its own stores."
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker bets its future" overstates the update. Forty stores and 300-plus locations are meaningful, but the facts do not say Warby is betting its future on retail.
"retail beats online-only for this company" abuses the evidence. The update says retail customers spend more than online-only customers, not that retail as a channel beats online overall.
"testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a comparison. The fact supplied is only a pharmacy-chain sales pilot.
"declining to break out exam revenue" turns a missing breakout into an active refusal. That is a financial-scrutiny angle, but the wording needs to stay cleaner.
gaps_in_B: "expansion bet is on eye exams, not frames" is too strong. The facts say most new stores will offer exams; they do not say exams are the strategic or revenue center.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for a publicly traded retailer. This is capital allocation or public-company retail finance, not funding mechanics.
"built its brand on skipping the middleman" and "made direct-to-consumer eyewear a category" import outside Warby lore instead of staying inside the supplied update.
"it is the reason the whole expansion exists" overstates the retail-spend claim. The update gives the claim, not management's full causal rationale for the expansion.
